new_statements.quote: Unfortunately, Ward's discussion of stress does not go any deeper than suggesting stress is related to verb stems, and in fact, it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward32. [fn.32:] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. Faraclas (1984b) presents an analysis of Obolo incorporating phrasal stress. [p.47:] The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High (H) and Low (L) ... Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages.
new_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce A. 1991. Phonetic aspects of the Lower Cross languages and their implications for sound change. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh (vol. 1). hdl:1842/19642; open copy https://core.ac.uk/download/
new_statements.locator: Sec. 2.3.3.3, pp. 54-55 and fn. 32 p. 55 (PDF pp. 68-69); tone: sec. 2.2.2 p. 47 (PDF p. 61); Ebughu in the sample: p. 5 (PDF p. 19)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ebughu, like every Lower Cross language in Connell's sample, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep; falling tones arise by tone spreading (Connell 1994: 10). Connell finds no real evidence for word-level (verb-root) stress in Efik or the other LC languages, allowing only some form of phrasal stress and stress marking compound junctures. No source gives an Ebughu-specific stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is group-level (Efik and 'the other LC languages'), hedged ('likely some sort phrasal stress'), and Ebughu data were collected in 1988 without detailed cross-checking (p.11).
new_statements.domain_note: Word vs phrase: word-level stress denied evidence; phrase-level stress and compound-juncture stress conjectured. Tone characterization holds for lexical items in citation form (p.47); phrasal terracing described separately (Connell 1994: 10).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is group-level: Connell 1991 speaks of 'Efik or the other LC languages' and Ebughu (ebug1241) is one of the 19 languages of his sample (p.5; own 1988 field data). No Ebughu-specific phonological description exists; the only Ebughu-specific publication (Omego et al. 2012, semantics) is silent on stress and says the language is largely undocumented. Catalog entry would be 'Lower Cross group statement applied to Ebughu', same evidentiary basis as for Ito (itoo1242), Itu Mbon Uzo (itum1245) and the other small LC languages.

sources.citation: Omego, Christie, Ogbonna Anyanwu & Adimchinobi Onyegbuchulam. 2012. Verb-noun (object) selectional restriction in Ebughu. Theory and Practice in Language Studies 2(11): 2226-2238. doi:10.4304/tpls.2.11.2226-2238
sources.note: The only Ebughu-specific linguistic publication located. Verb-object semantics; abstract: 'Much is not known in documented forms about Ebughu and its speakers.' Examples unmarked for tone; 'stress', 'tone', 'accent' do not occur. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 1994. The Lower Cross languages: a prolegomena to the classification of the Cross River languages. Journal of West African Languages 24(1): 3-46.
sources.note: Sec. 3.3 p.10: every LC language has two tones H/L plus contrastive downstep; falling tones common in Ebughu (among others) from H-L-H tone spreading. Sec. 5 p.12: tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress rule for Ebughu.
